title: What do engineers do with computation?
text: No computer needed for this reading, and there won’t be one in Tuesday’s class either. We’re starting with the thing computers can’t do for you.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
Think First
Recall

Think of a time you gave someone instructions (directions to your house, a recipe, rules to a game) and they got it wrong. Whose fault was it?
In high school physics, you checked answers by asking “is this number reasonable?” — a car going 900 m/s is probably a mistake. What were you actually doing when you did that?

Look Ahead

If an AI can write working code from a plain-English description in five seconds, what’s left for the engineer to do?
What would it take for you to trust a program you didn’t write?
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Four things you may not know are possible with computation
text:
Four things you may not know are possible with computation
Predict every outcome of a process. Write a function that models something — the stress in a bracket, the temperature of a battery — then call it 100 times with 100 different inputs and write every result to a file. Runtime: about one second. You have just explored the entire design space of a product before building anything.
Handle data at engineering scale. A test rig logging 100 readings per second produces 360,000 rows an hour. Excel is not going to help you here. The tools in this course handle that with ease.
Reach out and touch the world. From a few lines of code you can pull the live position of the International Space Station, read the accelerometer inside your own phone, or send a question to an AI and use its answer inside your program.
Solve the unsolvable. Most real equations in engineering have no analytical solution. Many of those problems can be solved numerically in 10 lines of code.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The pipeline
Creating a computational tool looks something like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

The idea is always the hard part — no news there. But for the seventy years after that, production was the bottleneck: writing correct code takes time, and intro courses like this one were traditionally spent almost entirely on it.
That era is over. AI tools now produce working code from a good description in seconds. Production has, for most everyday engineering purposes, been solved.


John Backus reportedly disliked the tedium of assembly-language programming, so in the 1950s he led the team that created FORTRAN — and a generation of programmers stopped hand-writing machine instructions. Later, Python emerged as a much more readable language. The history of computer science is a story of making code less abstract, and LLMs might be the next step.
What should be the focus today?
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Specification means describing the problem completely
text:
Specification means describing the problem completely
… the inputs, the outputs, what should happen in between, and what should happen at the edges. It sounds trivial, but it is where real engineering projects most often fail: whether it’s an AI, a contractor, or a teammate who is helping with the task, every gap in your specification gets filled with an assumption. If your specification is doesn’t mention a material, maybe the ideal gas assumption is made — problematic when you are talking about oil flowing through a pipeline!
Try this one. A perfectly obedient, perfectly literal robot chef awaits your command:

“Make me a peanut butter sandwich.”







NoteClick to see what the robot needs to know





How many slices of bread? Which sides get peanut butter? How much? Spread with what? Should the jar be opened first? (You didn’t say.) Crusts on or off? Cut in half — diagonally? What if there’s no peanut butter: fail loudly, substitute almond butter, or go buy some? What does “done” look like?
None of these are jokes. Each is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the robot will — its way.



That’s a toy, so let’s do one that will actually happen to you in about three weeks. Same robot, same literalism, but now the request is one an engineer might really make:

“Tell me the average temperature in Boulder.”







NoteClick to see what the robot needs to know





Average over what — the whole century of records, one year, one month? Average of the daily highs, the daily lows, or the midpoint between them (which is what “average temperature” usually means, but you didn’t say)? What about the days the weather station didn’t report anything — and there are plenty of those, going back to the 1890s? In the raw file, a missing day isn’t blank, it’s -9999. Hand that to a robot that was told to average and it will average it, cheerfully, and tell you Boulder’s mean temperature is about −270 °C.
And units. The file stores temperatures in tenths of a degree Celsius. So a perfectly correct average of perfectly correct numbers is off by a factor of ten before you’ve done anything wrong.



Notice what’s different about that one. Nothing in it was a joke, every gap was a real decision, and — this is the part worth sitting with — a robot that filled those gaps badly would still hand you a number. A clean, confident, plausible-looking number. Somewhere between “Boulder averages 11 °C” and “Boulder averages −270 °C” there’s an answer that’s merely wrong, and that’s the dangerous one, because you’d never notice.
This is why we’re going to keep saying: a number isn’t an answer until someone has reasoned about it.
Now a different kind of gap. Compare these two problem statements:

A. “Write a function freq_shift(t, U, x0, y0, c, f) that returns the apparent frequency of a moving siren at each time in the array t, and plots it against time.”


B. “Write a program that would allow you to determine the velocity (speed and direction) of a siren.”

Statement A is a completed specification — someone already did all the thinking, and you’re just following instructions. Statement B is a problem. To attack B, you have to decide: what are the inputs? (A recording? Frequency-vs-time data?) What physics connects frequency to velocity? What are the unknowns? What should the program output, and in what form? What if the data is noisy?
In the old version of this course, where we focused on code production, you got Statement A. In this version, where we augment our work with LLMs, you get Statement B. Nobody in industry hands you Statement A; producing Statement A from Statement B is the job.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Verification means confirming a program does what you intended
text:
Verification means confirming a program does what you intended
… without taking anyone’s word for it, including the AI’s. This semester we will verify our code with:
The hand estimate: before running anything, compute a rough expected answer for one simple case. A dropped wrench falls 3 meters in about \(t = \sqrt{2h/g} \approx \sqrt{2(3~\text{m})/(9.8~\text{m/s}^2} \approx 0.8\) seconds. If the program says 12 seconds, the program is wrong. If it says 0.78 seconds, that’s a good sign.
The edge case: what happens at zero? At a negative input? When the file is empty? A program that works on the happy path and explodes at the edges is a program that will fail in the field.
The intuition check: you have years of physical intuition — heavier things don’t fall faster, sirens sound higher approaching than receding, hot coffee cools toward room temperature and not past it. That intuition is a verification instrument. Perhaps unexpectedly: we will be practicing our physical intuition in this programming course!






Important



An AI will hand you code that runs, produces a plot, and is confidently, invisibly wrong — a sign flipped, a unit mixed, an edge case botched. It will not warn you. “It ran without errors” and “it is correct” are entirely different claims, and confusing them is how engineering disasters happen.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The map of this course
Four verbs describe what engineers do with computation, and they outline this course:

Fetch — get real data into (and out of) your programs: sensors, files, the internet.
Process — turn raw data into meaningful quantities: functions, sweeps, big datasets.
Simulate — build models, make predictions, ask “what if,” and know when not to believe yourself.
Analyze — communicate findings honestly: good plots, stated uncertainty, defensible conclusions.

We’ll spend the most explicit time on Process and Simulate; Fetch and Analyze are woven through everything. The standards page lists what you’ll be able to do under each verb.






TipThink



The pipeline diagram above should look faintly familiar if you’ve seen an engineering design loop: define the problem, generate a solution, test it, iterate. That’s not a coincidence — specify/produce/verify/adapt is the design loop, wearing computational clothes. You are not learning “a programming class thing.” You are learning how engineers attack problems.



On paper (yes, actual paper), write a specification — 5 to 10 sentences — for this problem: a program that tells a student the fastest walking route between two buildings on campus. Your spec must state the inputs, the outputs, and at least three edge cases with what should happen in each.
Class opens with tables exchanging specs and hunting for the gaps. The table that finds the most unstated assumptions in another table’s spec wins bragging rights. Bring your sharpest pedantry.

title: Side Quests
text:
Once Base Camp winds down, Mondays keep going with a new flavor: Side Quests, for anyone who wants to go further than the course goes. Nothing here affects your grade, nothing is secretly required, nobody takes attendance — and by this point in the semester, Mondays are just the day we hang out and build things, which is roughly what engineering departments are for.
Dress rehearsals still claim the Mondays before checkpoints 3 and 4 (weeks 8 and 10); quests fill the rest. Which quests run is up to you — signups on Canvas; a quest runs if ~10 people want it — so consider this page a menu. Pitch new ones anytime; the best quests come from what you ask for. Every quest that runs leaves behind a one-page recipe on this site, so the menu grows into a library.

title: Side Quests
text:
The menu
Starting from scratch. (Timed for week 11, right before project launch.) The blank-page protocol: what to actually do when there’s no template, no starter code, and no instructions — which is your project in four days, and most of your career. The protocol is teachable: restate the problem in one sentence; name inputs and outputs; find the smallest version that could possibly work; build that; grow it. We’ll start something real from nothing, live, mistakes included.
Git & version control. (Week 12.) How real teams avoid final_v2_ACTUAL_final.py: commits, history, branches, and undo-anything confidence.
Build a tiny language model. You’ve directed LLMs all semester; now build the ancestor — a Markov text generator, ~30 lines. Feed it a book from Project Gutenberg, watch it babble plausibly.
Parametric design → 3D print. Code that generates geometry: a bracket with parameterized dimensions, swept over a design variable — and then we print the winner on the College’s machines. It’s HW 3’s parameter sweep made physical: the design space in your hand. (Print queue permitting.)

title: Practice Library
text:
Tracing (weeks 2–3)
T1. Look through the code and try to predict all three printed values, then run to check.







Make a two-column table of a and b values, then go line-by-line. Remember: = means is assigned — line 3 uses the values as they are at that moment.


10, 4, 6.

After line 1: a is 6.
After line 2: b is 4 (and a is still 6).
After Line 3: a is 6+4, that is: a is 10. (And b stays 4 — it stored a value, not a relationship.)


T2. This one prints a single value.







The same line twice is not the same result twice — the second one starts from where the first one left off.


16. First squaring: 4. Second squaring squares the new value: 16.

title: Practice Library
text:
Functions (week 3)
F1. Fill in the blank ______ so the function matches its docstring, then verify it works by running the code.







Area is π r² — and remember Python needs the power written explicitly.


return 3.14159 * r ** 2      # or: 3.14159 * r * r

F2. Predict what prints.







The n inside the function is limited in scope. What happens in the function stays in the function — only the return value escapes.


1 then 11. The outer n is untouched; add_ten worked on its own local copy and returned the result.

title: Practice Library
text:
Logic (week 4)
L1.







Go top to bottom, and the first true branch wins. Check the boundaries: is 100 greater than 100?


highway, highway (100 is not > 100), too fast, city (−5 falls through to else… not sure this was a good specification, if we are talking about the speed of a city!).

title: Practice Library
text:
Loops (week 5)
X1. Fix the loop so it prints the sum of the squares of 1 through 4. (What value do you expect?)







Run it as-is and look at what you get: 16. The loop isn’t accumulating — each pass throws away the previous total. What’s missing from the right-hand side?


total = total + k * k
The accumulator pattern: the new total is built from the old total. total = k * k just overwrites, and you end up with only the last pass (16).

X2. Assembly problem: these lines compute the average of a list, but they’re scrambled. Reorder them (cut and paste in the editor) so it runs and prints 5.0.








Names must exist before they’re used.
The indented line belongs to the for.
The print needs everything finished.

(Also — could you avoid hard-coding count = 3? Python’s len(values) exists and is probably better.


values = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
count = 3
for v in values:
    total = total + v
print(total / count)
The first three lines can go in any order among themselves.

title: Practice Library
text:
Arrays (weeks 5–6)
A1. Fill in the blank so t holds the fall time for every height at once, then print it.







The formula is \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}\), and NumPy’s square root is np.sqrt(...). Write the arithmetic as if h were a single number — the array handles the “for every value” part itself.


t = np.sqrt(2 * h / 9.81)
The first entry should be ≈ 0.45 s and each height is 4× the previous, so each time should be 2× the previous (√4 = 2).

title: How your grade works
text:
Your grade is built from exactly two ingredients:
There are no points, no weighted averages, no partial credit, and no curve. Maybe most interesting: you can recover if you struggle early and still receive an A grade!

title: How your grade works
text:
Standards: Met or Not Yet
Every standard gets multiple opportunities across the semester (checkpoints, in-class work, the project, the defense — the schedule shows where each appears). The rules:

Convergent standards (the ones with checkable right answers) require two successful demonstrations on different occasions.
Divergent standards (open-ended) require one demonstration at “Meets” quality, with the right to revise and resubmit once per artifact.
“Not Yet” means you aren’t there yet. But if you are Not Yet on a standard in week 4, then successfully demonstrate it in week 11, the standard is Met and you will receive full credit. (Though don’t forget some standards require two successful demonstrations.)
Reassessment happens at the scheduled reappearances of each standard, plus token-purchased retries — see Tokens.


Checkpoints
Four Tuesdays (weeks 4, 6, 8, and 10) open with a checkpoint: about twenty minutes, individual, on paper, no AI, no notes. Each checkpoint assesses a few convergent standards and re-offers items from earlier checkpoints. 

Expect to produce a short function by hand from a given spec — five lines or so, no AI. Why, in a course that delegates production to LLMs, are we having you write code yourself from scratch? Because verification requires an understanding of coding elements/what is possible with computing and at least a bit of fluency with the language.

title: How your grade works
text:
Engagement credits: the process
Part of your grade will be based on before-class preparation and in-class collaboration. These won’t be graded on correctness, and instead are based on good-faith completion:

Rules: a wrong answer with detailed reasoning earns full credit; a blank or a transparently rushed scribble earns none. Credits are earned in class and can’t be replaced with out of class work (though you can safely miss a few, and tokens can be used as a pressure-release valve).

Project-period credits are individual
The 8 credits of the project period (pin-ups #1 and #2, the mock defense) are awarded per person, informed by teammate evaluation — two short, description-based evaluations, one formative in week 13 and one summative in finals week. The default outcome is nothing: ordinary teams keep ordinary credits. The instrument exists for the teammate no one can describe. Full mechanics, including exactly what the form asks and why it asks for descriptions rather than ratings, on the peer evaluation page.

title: How your grade works
text:
Tokens
Everyone starts the semester with 3 tokens. Spend one for: a 48-hour deadline extension; an excused activity (the engagement credits without attending — illness, interviews, life); or one extra reassessment of a convergent standard outside its scheduled windows. No questions asked, no documentation required. Unspent tokens convert to 1 engagement credit each at semester’s end.

Minus: exactly one requirement falls short of your row, and it lands in the row directly below → you get the higher grade with a minus rather than dropping a full letter. F is reserved for missing the D row.
Why P5 is necessary for the A and B: P5 — holding your whole project in your head — is what the defense measures, and it’s the standard that certifies all the others were yours. An A in a course about directing and auditing computation, held by someone who can’t explain their own project, would be a false statement. We don’t issue those.

title: How your grade works
text:
Three worked examples
Student 1 — the straightforward case. Meets 14 standards including P5 (only S4 still Not Yet after the project), earns 43 engagement credits, spends one token on an extension during a brutal midterm week. Check the A row: 14 ≥ 14 ✓, P5 ✓, 43 ≥ 40 ✓. Grade: A. The two unspent tokens add 2 credits (45), which changes nothing.
Student 2 — the slow start (read this one if you’re nervous). Bombs the first checkpoint: P1 and P4 both Not Yet in week 4, and it feels catastrophic. It isn’t — both standards are re-offered at the week-6 and week-8 checkpoints, and Student 2 demonstrated each twice by mid-semester. Finishes with 12 standards Met including P5 (S2 and A3 fell short on the project report; his revision closed A3 but not S2, and F1 never came together). Then 41 engagement credits, did the work all semester even while the checkpoints were rough. B row: 12 ≥ 12 ✓, P5 ✓, 41 ≥ 32 ✓ → at least a B. Plus check: meet ≥ 1 requirement of the A row? The 41 credits clear the A row’s 40 ✓. Grade: B+. Note the early disasters cost nothing. The grade records where we ended up.
Student 3 — the ghost (read this one if you’re planning to skip class). Brilliant, and knows it: 13 standards Met including P5, some on first attempt. But treats class as optional — skips the readings’ commitments, misses most Thursdays — and finishes with 22 engagement credits, having spent no tokens (which convert: 22 + 3 = 25). B row: standards ✓ ✓, but 25 < 32 ✗. C row: 13 ≥ 10 ✓, 25 ≥ 24 ✓ → at least a C. Plus check: meets two B-row requirements (standards, P5) → Grade: C+. Is that harsh for someone with 13 standards? Well, this course is also about the process — prepare, commit, argue, critique. Ten more Thursdays of just participating and we’re at a B+.

title: Welcome
text:
Welcome to MCEN 1030: Introduction to Engineering Computing, taught by Professor Jeremy Koch in the Fall 2026 semester.
When I took this course (in fall 2006… oof), the big challenge for students was to figure out how to use fundamental programming ideas — loops, conditional statements, indexing — to achieve an engineering task. My professor gave very clean problem statements so that we could focus on writing the code, and we spent hours figuring out how to put the ideas in the right order, getting the syntax right, and debugging errors.
Today, we have AI (artificial intelligence), specifically LLMs (large language models). These have proven to be extremely capable of writing code based on a prompt (natural language instructions). Engineers need some understanding of how computation can be used in their projects, but they are not manually typing in for i in items: anymore… they are writing prompts that include something like “iterate through the items in that list” and having an LLM do the work.
What does that mean for an introduction to engineering computing class, if traditional problems have been conquered by AI? We still need to learn what is possible with computation (can we solve “unsolvable” differential equations like The Lorenz Equations?), how computer logic works (a=5,b=a+5,a=10… what is the current value of b?), and how to interpret code (what is happening with for i in items:?), but we will also learn how to integrate LLMs into our workflow. Importantly, we are not going to treat LLM-generated code as a “black box”: we need to understand what is going on in our code. After all, if you end up using an LLM-generated result in your job and something explodes, you won’t be able to blame an LLM — it’s your fault!
Further, we’ll learn why LLMs are not 100% trustworthy and will see that they, too, often produce broken code. That doesn’t mean we give up on the project — if we understand how to talk about computational ideas, how to interpret results, and how to troubleshoot/debug, LLMs are tool that can help us produce better work, faster, even if their initial result is flawed. And they’ll give us an opportunity to do some moderately ambitious engineering work this semester.

title: Welcome
text:
The big idea
The process of creating computational tools looks roughly like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

For decades, Production — thinking about the code elements, structure, and syntax, and doing the typing — was the bottleneck, and so intro courses like this one spent nearly all their time on it. That bottleneck is gone: AI tools produce working code from a good description in seconds. The new bottlenecks are the two highlighted boxes:
Specification means describing the problem precisely: the inputs and outputs, what has to happen in the middle, what to do at the edges. If you can’t articulate the problem, no tool — human or AI — can solve it for you.
Verification means refusing to trust a black box: sanity-checking results against hand estimates, testing edge cases, knowing the ways a program (or a model, or an AI) goes wrong.
You will still read and run and modify plenty of code in this course — you can’t verify what you can’t read. But you will be graded on whether you can think computationally: frame a problem, direct the tools, and audit the results. That is what engineers actually do!

title: Welcome
text:
How a week works
Before class, you’ll read one lesson on this site (~30 minutes). Most of the code on these pages executes right in your browser and is editable. Every lesson ends with a Bring to class box: one question you answer on paper before you arrive.


More serious coding will happen in Google Colab, MATLAB Online, or Python/MATLAB on your own machine — the getting going page has instructions.
Four Tuesdays open with a checkpoint (weeks 4, 6, 8, 10): twenty minutes, individual, on paper, no AI. Everything about how that feeds your grade is on the grading page.

The rest of class is work at the tables. Early in the semester that’s mostly short problems with right answers, later it shifts toward open-ended problems.
Get extra practice on Mondays (optional). TBase Camp early (the beginner on-ramp, checkpoint practice, …), Side Quests later (build a tiny language model, 3D-print a parameter sweep, …). No grades attached.
Homework problems are mostly about real mechanical engineering and will be formatted to include four steps: specify, annotate, verify, report. The homework page explains the format.

title: Welcome
text:
AI policy
You are expected to use AI tools in this course. You are also completely responsible for everything they produce for you. Every assignment asks you to show your specification, annotate the generated code, and demonstrate your verification.

title: Welcome
text:
Grading
This course uses standards-based grading: a list of specific skills (the standards), each marked Met or Not Yet, plus engagement credits for preparation and in-class work. There is no partial credit, no point-scrounging, and no penalty for struggling early: you can demonstrate a standard later when it reappears, and your grade is where you end up, not where you started. See the grading page.

title: Welcome
text:
Where to go next
The schedule shows the whole semester at a glance. Your first reading (for Tuesday) is What do engineers do with computation? You might look at Base Camp if you are new to coding and a bit nervous — the first few sessions designed to start you on the right foot. If curious, you might browse the Side Quests — a few ideas are already on that page.

title: Base Camp
text:
Mondays are an optional session/office hour. The first half of the semester, those Mondays are Base Camp: particularly useful if you are new to all of this, but open to everyone. No attendance is taken, nothing here affects your grade in any direction, but you will have a better grasp of the material at the end of each session. Plus, it’s a good way to meet some more people in the class and to talk to me/the TA!
Time and room set by signup poll in week 1 — watch Canvas.

title: Base Camp
text:
The sessions
BC1 (Week 1) · The computer itself, and how to talk about code. Before any coding: the computer itself. Browsers vs. apps, Colab login, where a downloaded file goes, folders, uploading to Colab, what “the cloud” means for your work. Then the second half: how to ask a question about code — the vocabulary (what do you call **, [], :?), the best way to ask a question: what I ran / what I expected / what I got instead. 
BC2 (Week 2) · First contact, slowly. The week 2 lesson again at half speed: cells, variables, running your first program, and learning to read error messages as information instead of accusation.
BC3 (Week 3) · The vocabulary drill. Reps on the core reading skills: trace variables by hand, predict outputs, read = as “is assigned.” Includes assembly problems — working code with its lines scrambled.
BC4 (Week 4) · Dress rehearsal: Checkpoint 1. A full practice checkpoint under real conditions — paper, timed, no AI — then we rework it together, item by item. 
BC5 (Week 5) · Loop clinic. Loops trip up more beginners than any other fundamental ingredient. Extra reps with accumulators, range, predicting iteration by hand, and loop assembly.
BC6 (Week 6) · Dress rehearsal: Checkpoint 2 — including re-offer items from Checkpoint 1, just as Tuesday will.

title: Getting going in your language
text: A few recommendations. You can do this entire course in Google Colab and MATLAB Online — nothing to install, works on any machine. But at some point you might decide running Python/MATLAB on your own machine is a good idea. Programs run faster, you can see all the files in a project easier, and it just feels better to have everything in a real editor.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Python via Google Colab
Go to colab.research.google.com, sign in with your university Google account, click New notebook, and… that’s it. Python runs on Google’s computers; NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are pre-installed. Notebooks are saved on your Google Drive. It is a little bit clumsy to handle files (e.g. a csv) but we will figure it out!

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Python on your machine
There are multiple avenues here, and if you are confident enough to find your own way (e.g., with pip), I believe in you.
There are two things you’ll need to do: install Python+a package manager, and install an editor.

Package manager
My recommendation is to install miniconda — NOT the full Anaconda (which you can find nearby if you really want to, but I’m not linking it). ::: {.column-margin} The full Anaconda is attractive: it has everything you will need in one install, but also a lot of unnecessary stuff. I grew to hate the navigator and the way it insisted on cross-checking all the packages every time I updated, and so I “downgraded” to miniconda (which still cross-checks, but there are way fewer packages). Additionally, I am not fond of the IDEs (Integrated Development Environment) that come with Anaconda. I much prefer VS Code, which supports Jupyter Notebooks and has a GitHub integration. :::
Miniconda installs Python, but otherwise I think there are zero packages, so you’ll install what you need from the command line. NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are necessary for this course; this page has the instructions. Note that miniconda still uses conda as the command.


What are “packages”? They are collections Python files that include useful Python functions that can be “called”. For example: someone has already written an implementation of the Trapezoid Rule for finding the area under a curve, and implemented it into the SciPy package. Now, instead of writing the code from scratch, you can just call that function with trapezoid(y) in your code.

pip is another package-management option — really not that different from conda. If you have reason to go that way, do it; plenty of tutorials around.







Tip



Some other packages that might be worth installing:

Jupyter is a “notebook” environment that looks a lot like Colab.
Seaborn is built on-top of matplotlib… it makes really beautiful plots.
SciPy is a toolbox of numerical routines — differential equation solvers, integrators, etc. It is a very large package but has a lot of very good tools that are used in engineering.
Scikit-learn is a good machine learning toolbox, we might use it in a Machine Learning Side Quest.





Editor
For the editor, I recommend VS Code — it supports Jupyter notebooks (and the notebook interface is better than the default Jupyter interface), has an integrated terminal, and has GitHub integration. Install VS Code, then its Python and Jupyter extensions (VS Code will automatically offer to install them the first time you open a .py or .ipynb file).
If you would like to install a different editor, and feel confident in doing so, go ahead! One example: Google Antigravity is apparently quite similar to VS Code. (I haven’t tried it yet!)






NotePython “environments” (optional reading)





Many serious programmers insist each project should have its own “environment” with a unique set of packages. For example, TensorFlow apparently does not play nice with NumPy version 2.0 or higher, and so folks who use TensorFlow will likely have an isolated environment for it where NumPy 1.9x is installed. (Even after reverting to NumPy 1.9x, I still couldn’t get TensorFlow to work, but that is beside the point!) For this class, it should not be a big deal to work entirely in the base environment.
If you do want to create separate environments, e.g., one for each project, you can. From the command line, you would start with something like conda create --name project1 and then conda activate project1 puts you in that environment, and then conda install numpy would get you numpy in just that environment. You need to install packages in each environment – if you have three environments set up on your machine, you might technically have NumPy installed three times.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
MATLAB (later in the semester)
As a CU student you have free access: create a MathWorks account with your CU email — instructions are here, under the student “How to get it.”
Once your account is tied to the school’s license, you can install desktop MATLAB or use MATLAB Online in the browser — students have used both, and you can hop back and forth. I like the immediacy of a local install and it runs a bit faster; Online gives you your code from any computer. For our purposes, either is fine.
Basic MATLAB is all this course needs; no toolboxes required. If you’re going on in the department, toolboxes like Simulink (used in System Dynamics) can be added anytime, so there’s no need to decide now.
The MathWorks “MATLAB Onramp” tutorial — find it under Online Training at matlab.mathworks.com — is genuinely good, takes about two hours.

title: The Standards
text:
Your grade in this course is built from the standards below. Each is a specific, demonstrable skill, marked met or not yet — there is no partial credit. Standards can be demonstrated (and re-demonstrated) through homework cycles, the in-class checkpoints (weeks 4, 6, 8, 10 — see grading), activity work, the design project, and the final defense. Convergent standards require at least one in-class demonstration. A standard missed in week 4 and nailed in week 11 is met.
Each standard carries a tag:

title: The Standards
section: Fetch — get real data in and out
text:
Fetch — get real data in and out
F1 — Acquire real data from a phone sensor, a file, or a keyless API. divergent
F2 — Read data’s shape: recognize CSV rows/columns and JSON/dictionary structure, and pull out the value you want. convergent

title: The Standards
section: Process — turn raw data into meaning
text:
Process — turn raw data into meaning
P1 — Write and reuse a function, and check it in isolation against a hand estimate. convergent (At least one P1 demonstration is hand-written at a checkpoint: a short function from a given spec, no AI — the minimum writing fluency that verification rests on.)
P2 — Run a parameter sweep: one function across many values, results written to a file. convergent
P3 — Tame a large dataset with pandas: filter, summarize, reduce many rows to a few meaningful numbers. convergent
P4 — Read code well enough to predict what a short script does, and recognize the shape of a computational project (inputs → script → outputs). convergent
P5 (proposed — under discussion) — Hold a whole project in your head: navigate a multi-file program you produced, and explain what each piece does, why it is structured that way, and what breaks if an input is malformed. divergent


P5 is what the final defense tests. P4 is reading a paragraph; P5 is knowing your way around the whole book.

title: The Standards
text:
Simulate — build models, make predictions
S1 — Build a model of a simple system: a given algebraic relation, or by time-stepping. convergent
S2 — Decide what to include and what to ignore: identify a model’s assumptions and judge whether they’re reasonable for the situation. divergent
S3 — Judge whether to trust the model: recognize the ways it goes wrong — too coarse a step (numerical), a missing effect (physical), or use outside its valid range (extrapolation). convergent
S4 — Explore with a model: pose a what-if, vary inputs, and interpret how the output responds. divergent

title: The Standards
section: Analyze — and the habits woven through everything
text:
Analyze — and the habits woven through everything
A1 — Estimate and sanity-check a result before trusting it. convergent
A2 — Make and judge an honest plot, and catch a misleading one. convergent
A3 — State uncertainty and document provenance: report how far model and reality diverge without false precision, and record where a number came from so someone else could rerun it. divergent
A4 — Direct and audit AI: get an AI to produce a computational artifact and critically audit the output. divergent
